title: First close-up look at asteroid NASA knocked off course – this week
excerpt: ESA is about to reveal a close-up look at the asteroid hit by NASA in a historic test of Earth's planetary defenses.
content:
Humanity is about to get its first close-up look at an asteroid since NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into it and changed its path through space.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has arrived at the Didymos asteroid system after a journey of about two years. On Wednesday, November 25, ESA is due to unveil Hera's first close-up images of Dimorphos, the small asteroid that was struck by NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test, or DART, in 2022.

The images could help scientists understand exactly what happened when DART slammed into Dimorphos and whether deliberately hitting an asteroid could be used to protect Earth one day.

Read More on News

Hera launched on October 7, 2024. Its main purpose is to closely examine Dimorphos and its much larger companion, Didymos, and study the effects of the DART collision. ESA says the findings should help turn the DART experiment into a technique that could be repeated if an asteroid threatening Earth were discovered in the future.

...

Ian Carnelli, who oversees ESA's Hera mission, previously said: “DART and Hera were originally conceived on a coordinated double-spacecraft basis, with one mission to perform the deflection and the other to perform precision measurements of the result.”

Newsweek has contacted Carnelli for comment.

Didymos and Dimorphos form what’s known as a binary asteroid system, meaning two asteroids travel together, with the smaller one circling, or orbiting, the larger one.

...

Didymos is about 780 meters across, roughly the same size as the Burj Khalifa, while Dimorphos measures about 151 meters across, which is a similar size to the Eiffel Tower, according to the ESA.

Dimorphos travels around Didymos at about three-quarters of a mile away from the larger asteroid's surface. Before DART arrived, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to complete one trip around Didymos.

Why Did NASA Crash Into an Asteroid?

On September 26, 2022, NASA deliberately smashed the DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at roughly 14,000 miles per hour.

The collision was the world's first full-scale test of technology designed to alter an asteroid's movement through space. The idea is relatively simple: if scientists discovered an asteroid that was on course to hit Earth far enough in advance, deliberately hitting it with a spacecraft could give it a small push. Over time, that small change could potentially cause the asteroid to miss Earth.

Neither Didymos nor Dimorphos posed a danger to Earth; instead, NASA used the asteroid system to test whether deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could change its path.

“This mission shows that NASA is trying to be ready for whatever the universe throws at us,” NASA Administrator Bill Nelson said.

The experiment worked. Observations showed that the collision shortened the time Dimorphos takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes, making Dimorphos the first object in the solar system to have its movement measurably changed by humans.

But scientists haven’t yet been able to examine the aftermath from close range.

NASA said the DART collision threw over two million pounds (one million kilograms) of the dusty rock into space – enough to fill six or seven rail cars, and the change to its orbit was greater than scientists had predicted. Hera will now investigate why the collision had such a strong effect and examine what it did to the asteroid itself.

Among the questions scientists hope to answer are what Dimorphos is like beneath its surface, how its shape was affected by the crash, and exactly how efficiently DART transferred its movement to the asteroid. ESA has previously said the collision may have created a crater around 20 meters across, although that’s one of the things Hera's observations will help to establish.

Where Can the New Images Be Seen?

...

ESA will reveal the first close-up images of Dimorphos during a livestream next week, on Wednesday, November 25.

Members of the public will be able to watch the unveiling through ESA WebTV and ESA's YouTube channel, and ESA's website will also show coverage of the images.

Scientists have already received close-up imagery of the larger Didymos from Hera, but Dimorphos was largely hidden in its shadow. Wednesday's release is expected to provide the first detailed close-up view of the smaller asteroid since DART captured images during the final seconds before crashing into it in 2022.

Newsweek has contacted the ESA press office for comment.
